issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette:
Mina Lim had been married for six years when she finally described, in fragments, the years she had spent with a former partner who began with charm and ended with control and physical abuse. She had met him when she was younger and eager to please, and by the time the violence started it was already hard for her to tell where persuasion ended and coercion began. What she remembered most vividly was not one single blow but the humiliating way he used his body to overrule hers: gripping her wrist hard enough that his fingers burned cold through her skin, pinning her in place when she tried to leave a room, brushing against her in anger with a touch that made her stomach drop before he even spoke. In the sessions, Mina could not describe the abuse in a straight line. When she tried, she would lose the thread halfway through, stare at the floor, and say she felt flooded all over again, as if the scene were happening in the office rather than years ago. The memory did not sit in the past for her; when it came back, her chest tightened and her body reacted with the same helplessness she had felt then. Each time the scene broke through again, Mina’s first thought was that there must be something deeply wrong with her for still being overtaken by it, and that this said something permanent about who she was.

What deepened Mina’s distress was how quickly the memory turned into judgment. She had come to believe the violence happened because of the way she acted, because she had been too soft, too accommodating, too slow to leave. She spoke about herself with a flat, pained certainty, saying there must be something wrong with her as a person for having stayed, for not seeing it sooner, for letting herself be treated that way. Beneath that was a humiliation she described as permanent, as though the shame had settled into her and changed how she understood herself. When the memory surged, that shame was immediate: the more vividly the scenes returned, the more she felt defective and exposed, and the more she concluded that the abuse said something enduring about who she was.

Those beliefs were woven into the habits that took over her days. Mina dwelled on how she used to be before the event, comparing herself to the woman she had been before she became so cautious and inward. She also spent long stretches trying to work out how it could have been prevented, turning the same moments over and over in her mind after work and late at night, asking what she should have noticed, what she should have done differently, where the first turning point had been. Because she felt responsible and ashamed, these thoughts became her way of making sense of what had happened, yet they also kept her close to it. After those evenings of replaying and blaming herself, Mina became stricter and narrower in how she lived: she cut short plans, avoided being alone with unfamiliar people, and kept herself busy rather than sit still long enough for the images or questions to catch up with her. When she replayed the abuse, the old scenes became more reachable, and the more she lived in those memories, the more convinced she became that her own actions had invited the harm and that there was something fundamentally wrong with her. That self-blame also made her especially alert to anything that could echo the loss of control she had lived through. At her physical therapy job, where she works hands-on with patients all day, she became increasingly tense when a patient reached unexpectedly, when someone stepped into her personal space, or when a clinician asked her to do something in a brusque, forceful tone. A specific temperature on the skin could jolt her badly too; the cold edge of a treatment pack, or a patient’s hand that felt unexpectedly chilly during an exam, could send her mind straight back to being held and overpowered. After those moments, she would refuse to let the feeling linger, hurrying through the rest of the appointment, avoiding any extra contact, and telling herself it was safer to stay brisk and detached than to risk being caught off guard again.

Mina’s beliefs made these moments harder to escape. If she felt there was something wrong with her, then any touch could seem like proof that she was still vulnerable, and any request that left her little choice could feel like the beginning of another loss of autonomy. Even ordinary contact at work became loaded with threat, because she was watching for dangerous people and reading caution into unfamiliar faces, dominant tones, or sudden movements. She started keeping conversations brief, standing at a distance when she could, and mentally scanning patients, coworkers, and strangers for signs that someone might overstep. That vigilance spread beyond the clinic; she was less open in social settings, more guarded with her husband, and often exhausted by the effort of staying prepared. The more she monitored people for danger, the more each unfamiliar touch or forceful instruction stood out to her, and the more it confirmed her sense that the world was full of menacing intent and that she herself was somehow marked by what had happened. Because she had come to see herself as marked and unsafe, Mina started interpreting ordinary moments as warning signs — a hand lifted to get her attention, a stranger standing too close in a hallway, a sharp tone from a coworker — and those cues were enough to send her into the same guarded, avoidant stance all over again. Having decided that she was marked and that other people could not be trusted to respect her boundaries, Mina kept her distance, cut conversations short, and worked hard to stay alert before anyone could get close enough to make her feel powerless again.

By the time Mina sought help, she was frightened by how little her efforts had reduced the pull of the memories or the grip of the shame. She came in after a week in which a patient’s unexpectedly cold hand during a transfer, followed by a supervisor pressing her to change schedules, left her shaking in the supply room and unable to finish documenting her notes. What brought her to treatment was the fear that she could no longer keep doing her work, or keep living as if constant alertness were the only way to stay safe. More than anything, she hoped to stop feeling humiliated and broken whenever the past surfaced, and she was afraid that if the memories kept arriving with the same force, she would never again feel fully in charge of her own body.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows reminders eliciting vigilance and scanning, but not a clear causal link from triggers to specific maladaptive strategies being driven by the triggers within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows reminders activating threat and vigilance, but it does not clearly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals or self-blaming beliefs in the same paragraph.
It states that beliefs make the moments harder to escape, but it does not clearly show negative appraisals causing the maladaptive coping strategies described.
The vignette shows self-blame increasing alertness to reminders, but it does not clearly depict negative appraisals producing triggers themselves.
The memory is said to turn into judgment, but the paragraph does not explicitly show the intrusive memory causing the negative appraisals as a causal relationship.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows reminders eliciting vigilance and scanning, but not a clear causal link from triggers to specific maladaptive strategies being driven by the triggers within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows reminders activating threat and vigilance, but it does not clearly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals or self-blaming beliefs in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: It states that beliefs make the moments harder to escape, but it does not clearly show negative appraisals causing the maladaptive coping strategies described.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows self-blame increasing alertness to reminders, but it does not clearly depict negative appraisals producing triggers themselves.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The memory is said to turn into judgment, but the paragraph does not explicitly show the intrusive memory causing the negative appraisals as a causal relationship.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
